title: Chemical Bonds and Properties of Compounds
seo_title: Chemistry 1: Chemical Bonds and Properties of Compounds Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
short_title: bonding, Lewis structures, VSEPR and polarity
standard_code: Chemistry 1, Quarter 2: Compounds and Their Formulas
standard_text: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds; electronegativity and polarity; molecular shapes (VSEPR); intermolecular forces; how bonding explains the properties of compounds. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, Chemistry 1, Quarter 2)
meta_desc: Free Chemistry 1 worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Quarter 2): ionic and covalent bonds, bonding and properties, vSEPR shapes, electronegativity and polarity and intermolecular forces. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Electron pairs push apart to give molecular shape.
key_sub: Polar bonds plus an uneven shape give a polar molecule.
body_html:
How to think about it

Ionic bonds form when electrons transfer from a metal to a non-metal; covalent bonds share electron pairs; metallic bonds have a sea of electrons. A Lewis structure shows the valence electrons around each atom.

VSEPR theory: electron pairs around a central atom repel, giving shapes such as linear (CO₂), trigonal planar (BF₃), tetrahedral (CH₄), trigonal pyramidal (NH₃) and bent (H₂O). A difference in electronegativity makes a bond polar; a polar molecule has an uneven charge, which affects intermolecular forces and boiling points.

Example

What is the shape of NH₃?

3 bonds + 1 lone pair

Answer: trigonal pyramidal

Example

Is CO₂ polar?

Polar bonds, but a linear shape

Answer: no, the dipoles cancel

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting lone pairs when choosing a shape.
  • Thinking every molecule with polar bonds is polar.
  • Mixing up intramolecular bonds and intermolecular forces.

faq.a: Oxygen has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, which push the bonds together.

faq.q: Why does water have a high boiling point?
faq.a: Its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.

items.q: What is the formula of magnesium nitride?
items.e: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is Mg<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium sulfide?
items.e: Potassium forms K<sup>+</sup> and sulfur forms S<sup>2−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the formula of sodium phosphide?
items.e: Sodium forms Na<sup>+</sup> and phosphorus forms P<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: How does a nitrogen atom (proton number 7) form an ion?
items.e: Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

items.q: What is the formula of barium nitride?
items.e: Barium forms Ba<sup>2+</sup> and nitrogen forms N<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: Na<sup>+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 2 × (+1) + 1 × (−2) = 0.

items.q: What is the formula of strontium phosphide?
items.e: Strontium forms Sr<sup>2+</sup> and phosphorus forms P<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the formula of barium iodide?
items.e: Barium forms Ba<sup>2+</sup> and iodine forms I<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the formula of sodium fluoride?
items.e: Na<sup>+</sup> and F<sup>−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is NaF.

items.q: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and P<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+2) + 2 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between aluminum (Al) and chlorine (Cl)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What is the formula of aluminum sulfide?
items.e: Al<sup>3+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is Al<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between barium (Ba) and fluorine (F)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What is the formula of sodium sulfide?
items.e: Sodium forms Na<sup>+</sup> and sulfur forms S<sup>2−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the formula of the ion formed by aluminum?
items.e: Aluminum (Z = 13) loses 3 electrons.

items.q: What is the formula of sodium chloride?
items.e: Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is NaCl.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between strontium (Sr) and fluorine (F)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between iodine (I) and fluorine (F)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between phosphorus (P) and bromine (Br)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Al<sup>3+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is graphene?
c: a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal network
items.e: It is very strong and conducts electricity.

items.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
c: their ions move to the electrodes
they have a sea of delocalized electrons that can move through the lattice
items.e: Electrons carry the charge.

items.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?
c: solid ionic compounds have no ions
the ions are free to move only when molten or dissolved
items.e: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between lead (Pb) and sodium (Na)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between aluminum (Al) and nitrogen (N)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What is a nanomaterial?
c: a material with particles or structures 1–100 nm in size
a material more than 1 mm thick
items.e: Nanoparticles have a very large surface area to volume ratio.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between lithium (Li) and phosphorus (P)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between strontium (Sr) and nitrogen (N)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between carbon (C) and chlorine (Cl)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: it has weak forces between molecules
each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a giant network
items.e: All the strong covalent bonds must be broken.

items.q: How can pure water be obtained from sea water?
items.e: Water evaporates and condenses; salt is left behind.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between tin (Sn) and aluminum (Al)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium nitride?
items.e: Calcium forms Ca<sup>2+</sup> and nitrogen forms N<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: How can sand be separated from salt water?
items.e: Insoluble solids stay on the filter paper.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium iodide?
items.e: Calcium forms Ca<sup>2+</sup> and iodine forms I<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the formula of barium bromide?
items.e: Barium forms Ba<sup>2+</sup> and bromine forms Br<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between oxygen (O) and hydrogen (H)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: Why are metals malleable?
c: the ions repel each other strongly
layers of cations can slide over each other while the delocalized electrons keep holding them together
items.e: Metallic bonding is not directional.

items.q: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and I<sup>−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 1 × (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between sulfur (S) and hydrogen (H)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What is the bond angle in NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the bond angle in PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of NH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: What is the shape of SF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: seesaw.

items.q: Which molecule has a zero dipole moment even though its bonds are polar?
items.e: It is linear, so the bond dipoles cancel.

items.q: What is the shape of PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in C₆H₆ (each carbon)?
items.e: C₆H₆ (each carbon): sp².

items.q: What is the shape of SF<sub>6</sub>?
items.e: 6 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: octahedral.

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in CH₃COOH (the COOH carbon)?
items.e: CH₃COOH (the COOH carbon): sp².

items.q: What is the shape of CO<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: linear.

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in CO₂?
items.e: CO₂: sp.

items.q: What is the shape of CCl₄?
items.e: CCl₄: tetrahedral.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>2</sub>O?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: bent (non-linear).

items.q: What is the shape of SiCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the central atom in SF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: SF4: 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pairs.

items.q: What is the bond angle in BeCl<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of XeF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: square planar.

items.q: What is the bond angle in H<sub>2</sub>S?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>2</sub>S?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: bent (non-linear).

items.q: What is the shape of BeCl<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: linear.

items.q: Sulfur (S) has 6 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 2 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: In a bond between phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N) (electronegativities 2.19 and 3.04), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: Chlorine (Cl) has 7 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 1 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 1 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons; 3 are used in bonds, leaving 1 pairs.

items.q: How many covalent bonds does phosphorus (P) usually form?
items.e: It needs 3 more electrons for a full outer shell.

items.q: What is the order of repulsion in VSEPR theory?
c: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair
bond pair–bond pair > lone pair–lone pair
lone pair–bond pair is the largest
items.e: So bond angles shrink when lone pairs are present.

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in CH<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: Carbon has 4 valence electrons; 4 are used in bonds, leaving 0 pairs.

items.q: What is the formal charge on each oxygen in the O₃ structure O=O⁺–O⁻? (the ends)
c: 0 on the double-bonded end, −1 on the single-bonded end
items.e: Formal charge = V − L − ½B.

items.q: What is the shape of BF₃?
items.e: BF₃: trigonal planar.

items.q: Electronegativity: fluorine (F) = 3.98 and iodine (I) = 2.66. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.32. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: Which is more covalent, NaCl or LiCl?
items.e: Fajans' rules: the small Li⁺ polarizes Cl⁻ more.

items.q: Which molecule has an expanded octet?
items.e: Phosphorus has ten electrons around it.

items.q: In a bond between oxygen (O) and selenium (Se) (electronegativities 3.44 and 2.55), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: How many electrons are shared in a double covalent bond?
items.e: Each bond is one shared pair (2 electrons).

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in HCl?
items.e: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons; 1 are used in bonds, leaving 3 pairs.

items.q: Which molecule does NOT obey the octet rule?
items.e: Boron has only six electrons in BF₃.

items.q: What is the shape of ClF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: T-shaped.

items.q: How many σ and π bonds are there in ethyne, C₂H₂?
items.e: C≡C is one σ + two π; two C–H σ bonds.

items.q: Silicon (Si) has 4 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 4 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 4 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: Electronegativity: fluorine (F) = 3.98 and calcium (Ca) = 1.00. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 2.98. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.
